stops.name: Amarnath, the ice-lingam in the Himalaya
stops.campa: She climbs to the cave of Amarnath in the Kashmir heights, where each year an ice-lingam of Shiva rises and melts with the moon: the god of destruction and renewal, the Kali she loved as a child now in his male form, lord of the eternal dance. She keeps her pilgrimages to Gangotri, to the sources of the Ganges, to Mathura at the birth-festival of Krishna. In the wheel of the yugas she reads all history: the Golden Age long fallen, the Kali Yuga at its blackest, and the god who will end it not yet come.

stops.name: Delhi, the Hindu Mission, the wandering lecturer
stops.campa: She enlists in the Hindu Mission and becomes its travelling lecturer, carrying her gospel of Aryan blood and pagan renewal from town to town across the north. She meets Swami Satyananda; she meets Subhas Chandra Bose, whom she reveres as India's warrior-liberator. She teaches too at a college near the capital. To Hindu nationalism she brings the vocabulary of race and purity forged in Europe, and she preaches that India must not be submerged by the alien creeds: a doctrine she will set down as a warning to the whole people.

stops.name: Calcutta, 'A Warning to the Hindus'
stops.campa: At Calcutta the Hindu Mission publishes her Warning to the Hindus, with a preface by the elder Savarkar's brother. In it she proclaims Hindu India the last living fragment of the primordial Aryan spirit, and cries that it must guard its blood and its gods against Islam, against Christianity, against the leveling modern world. It is Europe's racial doctrine dressed in a sari and offered to Bharat as its own. The book makes her a name among the Hindu nationalists: a foreign priestess telling India to be, above all, Aryan.
stops.quote: The Hindus are the last great people on earth to have kept, along with their ancient tongue, the consciousness of the sacredness of blood and soil.

stops.name: Calcutta, marriage to Asit Krishna Mukherji
stops.campa: She weds Asit Krishna Mukherji, a Bengali Brahmin, editor, and open admirer of the Axis. First a civil bond in the autumn of thirty-nine, then on the ninth of June the sacred Hindu rite. Theirs is a marriage of the cause as much as the heart: through his New Mercury and his contacts they gather what serves the Axis, and she will boast that she helped Bose reach the Japanese. To the end she signs herself Savitri Devi Mukherji, keeping the Brahmin name as proof that her blood-faith found, in India, a true and lawful Aryan hearth.

stops.name: Sevagram, the half-hour with Gandhi
stops.campa: At Wardha she is granted half an hour with Gandhi in his ashram at Sevagram. The apostle of non-violence and the priestess of the lightning face each other across an unbridgeable gulf. She cannot abide his ahimsa toward the human world, his pity for the weak, his creed of the spinning-wheel; yet the same woman who scorns his mercy toward men has wept her life long over the suffering of animals. She leaves unmoved, certain that the age of pity must be burned away before the Golden Age can dawn.

stops.name: Varkala, despair on the shore, the war lost
stops.campa: The Reich is in ruins, the god she worshipped in a man is dead in Berlin, and the wheel has turned to its blackest hour. On the beach at Varkala she walks into the sea to end herself. But she does not die. She rises from the water resolved instead upon a mission: to keep the flame, to carry the faith through the long night, to prophesy the one who is still to come: the final avatar, Kalki, who will wield perfect lightning and perfect sun, and shatter the Dark Age at last.

stops.name: London, she carries the mission back to Europe
stops.campa: On a British-Indian passport she lands at Southampton and comes up to London, back into the wreck of the West. She lectures on Akhnaton, dances with Ram Gopal's Indian company to earn her bread, and visits her mother in France. But beneath the wandering scholar burns the postwar mission: to reach the defeated Germans, to tell them their faith is not dead but sleeping. She has already begun, from India, the two books that will fix her mythology forever: the indictment of man, and the great tripartite history of Time.

stops.name: London, 'The Impeachment of Man' finished
stops.campa: In the year after the war she completes the strangest of her books: an impeachment of the entire human race for its cruelty to the animals and the earth. Man, she declares, is no lord set above nature but a part of it, and a wicked part; the slaughterhouse, the vivisector's table, the felled forest are his true crimes, beside which he dares to prate of 'war crimes'. The gentleness she withholds from the weak among men she pours out upon the beast: the one strand of her creed the world can almost love, until it sees what it is bound to.

stops.name: Mount Hekla, a night on the burning mountain
stops.campa: Word comes that Hekla, the great volcano of Iceland, has awoken. She hurries north and, on the fourth of April, climbs onto the slopes of the erupting mountain and passes the night amid its fire and thunder. To her this is no natural curiosity but a sacrament: the Life-Force showing its true face, neither good nor evil, creating and destroying in one breath, the lightning and the sun made molten rock. Iceland, land of the old Germanic gods, gives her its burning mountain as a sign that the wheel still turns.

stops.name: Occupied Germany, the leaflets from the Nord Express
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of June she boards the Nord Express and rides through the shattered Reich, scattering thousands of handwritten leaflets from the windows and pressing them into hands: Men and women of Germany, hold fast to our glorious National Socialist faith, and resist! She sells her gold jewelry to pay for the printing of bills and posters. Through that summer she slips back in and out, at Saarbrücken and Cologne, pasting her creed upon the walls of the occupied land: a lone missionary of a banned religion in the ruins of its temple.
stops.quote: In distress and defeat, hold fast to our glorious National-Socialist faith and resist!
stops.quote_source: Handwritten leaflet distributed in occupied Germany, 1948 (recounted in Gold in the Furnace)

stops.name: Düsseldorf, the trial
stops.campa: Arrested at Cologne in February for posting her bills, she is brought on the fifth of April before a court at Düsseldorf under the Allied Control Council, charged with spreading National Socialist ideas on German soil. She does not repent; she glories in it, turning the dock into a pulpit. She is sentenced to three years. Far from breaking her, the arrest confirms her sense of destiny: she is the confessor of a persecuted faith, gold thrown into the furnace to be proved, and out of this trial will come her memoir Defiance.

stops.name: Werl, the prison, and the fellowship of the condemned
stops.campa: In the prison at Werl she seeks out her comrades and superiors, the war criminals of the fallen Reich, and finds among the women a friend in a former Belsen wardress. The crypto-Nazi guards indulge her, and she writes in a fever, pouring whole chapters of Gold in the Furnace and The Lightning and the Sun onto paper behind bars. To her the cell is a shrine and captivity an honour. Released in August after some six months, expelled toward India, she carries out the manuscripts that will become her testament.
stops.quote: This whole book was written in the joy of certitude — the certitude that our Ideology is bound to win in the end, whatever be, in the meantime, the fate of those who hold it.
